title: The Tower on the Marstall: Bode, the Gap at 28, and the Naming of Uranus
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Hamburg, birth in the merchant Altstadt
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day
stops.campa: Johann Elert Bode is born in Hamburg on the nineteenth of January, eldest of nine children of a merchant family. The street and the house are not preserved in any reachable record, and the pin marks the Altstadt generally, nothing narrower. His father keeps a commercial school and teaches the boy himself; there is no tutor and no plan for a university. Hamburg in 1747 is a free city of ledgers, tides and rope, and the child who will spend fifty years fixing the positions of stars learns his first arithmetic from a man counting cargo.
suggested_refs: The Hamburg Altstadt of the 1740s, the merchant quarter of Bode's childhood
sources: Deutsche Biographie entry, attempted and returned HTTP 404

stops.name: Hamburg, the eye that fails
stops.date_confidence: no year is given by any source; both the English and German biographies place the illness in his youth without date, and 1760 is an editorial midpoint of that youth, not an attested date
stops.campa: A severe illness in boyhood damages his right eye. The loss of vision is permanent, and he will observe, compute and engrave for the next sixty years with one good eye. No source names the disease and none names the year. The man who will publish a catalogue of more than seventeen thousand stars, and draw twenty copper plates of the constellations, first learns that the sky has to be taken in on half the terms other people get, and does not appear to have mentioned it again in anything that survives.
suggested_refs: The undated youthful illness of the right eye, reported without detail in both standard biographies

stops.name: Hamburg, Busch opens his library
stops.date_confidence: the year is attested; no month or day is recorded, defaulted to 01-01
stops.campa: At the Akademisches Gymnasium the boy is introduced to the mathematician Johann Georg Busch, who opens his library and his instruments to him. Bode attends no university and will never hold a degree. What he has instead is a borrowed telescope, a borrowed shelf and the habit of copying out what he cannot afford to own. The building the Gymnasium occupied in the 1760s could not be confirmed from any reachable source, and the pin approximates the Domplatz and Speersort quarter where the school stood.
suggested_refs: Johann Georg Busch's private library and instrument collection at Hamburg

stops.name: Hamburg, the eclipse of August
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day
stops.campa: On the fifth of August the sun is eclipsed over northern Germany, and the nineteen-year-old watches it and writes it up. The paper is his first published work. He holds no post at any observatory and nobody pays him. He has attended no university and holds no degree. He is a self-taught boy in a trading city with one working eye, and he has decided that what he sees is worth putting into print. Within six years the Prussian Academy of Sciences in Berlin will send for him by name.
suggested_refs: Bode's first publication, on the solar eclipse of 5 August 1766

stops.name: Hamburg, the Anleitung goes to press
stops.date_confidence: the year of the first edition is attested; no month recorded, defaulted to 01-01
stops.campa: Bode publishes Anleitung zur Kenntniss des gestirnten Himmels, a guide to the starry sky for readers who own no instrument. It will run to more than ten editions, the last recorded in 1844, and outlive its author by eighteen years. Whether this first edition already carried the footnote on planetary spacing is disputed: one line of sources puts the statement here in 1768, another puts Bode's version of the rule in the second edition of 1772. Both datings stand here together, unresolved.
suggested_refs: Anleitung zur Kenntniss des gestirnten Himmels, first edition, Hamburg 1768

stops.name: Hamburg, the transit of Venus and a comet shared
stops.date_confidence: the transit is attested to 3 June 1769; Bode's published account is attested to the year
stops.campa: Venus crosses the face of the sun on the third of June, the second transit of a pair that will not recur for over a century, and Bode publishes his account of it. The same year he takes independent sight of the comet catalogued as C/1769 P1, the one that carries Messier's name. He is twenty-two. From a private observing site in a merchant city, with no institution behind him and no salary at all, he has now done twice over what observatories are funded to do.
suggested_refs: The transit of Venus of 3 June 1769; comet C/1769 P1 (Messier)

stops.name: Hamburg, the comet that will be lost
stops.date_confidence: the comet is attested to 1770; the date of Bode's own observation is not recorded and the month is an editorial default
stops.campa: He observes the comet later catalogued as D/1770 L1, the one Anders Johan Lexell computes and that afterwards vanishes, thrown off its course by Jupiter and never seen again. Bode's last Hamburg comet is a body that stops existing as an observable object. Lexell, who will spend the last afternoon of Leonhard Euler's life discussing the orbit of a different new planet, is at this moment the man turning observations of Bode's kind into computed orbits.
suggested_refs: Comet D/1770 L1 (Lexell), lost after a close approach to Jupiter

stops.name: Berlin, called by Lambert to the Academy
stops.date_confidence: the year is attested; the month of the move is not recorded, defaulted to 01-01
stops.campa: Johann Heinrich Lambert brings him to Berlin to compute planetary ephemerides for the Prussian Academy of Sciences. Bode is twenty-five, holds no degree, and comes to do the arithmetic that keeps a calendar of the sky honest. He will spend the rest of his working life in the city, a few streets from the observatory tower he is about to climb.
suggested_refs: The Prussian Academy of Sciences under Lambert, which recruited Bode from Hamburg

stops.name: Berlin, the tower on the Marstall
stops.date_confidence: the year is attested; the month is an editorial default with no source behind it
stops.campa: The old Berlin Observatory is a tower twenty-seven metres high, raised between 1700 and 1711 by Martin Grunberg on the roof of the royal stables in Dorotheenstadt, on the foundation Gottfried Kirch began. Bode climbs into it as Lambert's computer and does not leave it for fifty-three years. Two of the sources consulted put the tower about a hundred metres apart, at 52.5189 and 13.3914 in one and 52.5177 and 13.3889 in the other; the discrepancy is recorded here rather than resolved.
suggested_refs: The Dorotheenstadt tower observatory on the royal Marstall, Berlin, built 1700-1711

stops.name: Berlin, the rule of the planetary distances
stops.date_confidence: the second edition of the Anleitung is attested to 1772; no month is recorded and September is an editorial default. Sources disagree over whether Bode first printed the rule in the 1768 Hamburg edition or here; the disagreement is not resolved
stops.campa: The second edition of the Anleitung carries the series that will bear his name. Take Saturn at 100: Mercury falls at 4, Venus at 7, Earth at 10, Mars at 16, then a gap at 28 where nothing has ever been seen, then Jupiter at 52 and Saturn at 100. Johann Daniel Titius had printed the relation in 1766 inside his German edition of Bonnet. Bode prints it without crediting him and adds the attribution only in later editions. The gap at 28 is the sentence the next thirty years will chase.
stops.quote: This latter point seems in particular to follow from the astonishing relation which the known six planets observe in their distances from the Sun. Let the distance from the Sun to Saturn be taken as 100, then Mercury is separated by 4 such parts from the Sun. Venus is 4+3=7. The Earth 4+6=10. Mars 4+12=16. Now comes a gap in this so orderly progression. After Mars there follows a space of 4+24=28 parts, in which no planet has yet been seen. Can one believe that the Founder of the universe had left this space empty? Certainly not. From here we come to the distance of Jupiter by 4+48=52 parts, and finally to that of Saturn by 4+96=100 parts.
stops.quote_source: Johann Elert Bode, Anleitung zur Kenntniss des gestirnten Himmels, 2nd ed. (Berlin, 1772), footnote; English translation by Michael Hoskin, 'Bode's Law and the Discovery of Ceres' (Osservatorio Astronomico di Palermo, 1992), as quoted in the Wikipedia article 'Titius-Bode law'
suggested_refs: Johann Daniel Titius's 1766 German translation of Charles Bonnet, where the relation first appears in print

stops.name: Berlin, the first Astronomisches Jahrbuch
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1774 for the volume computed for the year 1776; the apparent 1774-versus-1776 disagreement between sources is the same fact stated two ways
stops.campa: The first Berliner Astronomisches Jahrbuch appears, computed for the year 1776. The series is begun under Lambert's direction, and when Lambert dies in 1777 Bode takes it over outright and issues it for the rest of his life. Sources count the volumes he saw through differently, fifty-one in one and fifty-four in another, and put the series' end at 1957 or at 1959. On any of those counts it runs longer than any other publication in astronomy, and calling Bode its founder overstates what Lambert began.
suggested_refs: Berliner Astronomisches Jahrbuch, first volume, computed for 1776
sources: Allgemeine Deutsche Biographie, 'Bode, Johann Elert', via de.wikisource

stops.name: Berlin, marriage to Johanna Christina Lange
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day
stops.campa: He marries Johanna Christina Lange on the fourteenth of July. The church is not named in any reachable source, and the pin defaults to the observatory, the only Berlin address of his that is firmly fixed. Four children come of the marriage: Anna Ernestine Christine in 1775, Johann Christian August Wilhelm in 1777, Theodor Heinrich August in 1779, Johanna Dorothea Karoline in 1782. Three of the four he will bury. The yearbook goes out on time in each of those years.
suggested_refs: The Bode household in Dorotheenstadt, Berlin, 1774 onward

stops.name: Berlin, the last night of 1774 and two nebulae
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day
stops.campa: On the last night of the year Bode finds two faint patches in Ursa Major and records them as nebulae. They are galaxies some twelve million light years off, and they will be catalogued as Messier 81 and Messier 82; the brighter is still called Bode's Galaxy. He is looking out of the Dorotheenstadt tower with a damaged right eye at objects for which nobody in 1774 has a word. Messier lists them, Bode never learns what they are, and no one else does either for another century and a half.
suggested_refs: Messier 81 and Messier 82 in Ursa Major, discovered from the Berlin tower on 31 December 1774

stops.name: Berlin, the sun taken for a dark body
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1776 by volume and page; no month recorded, defaulted to 01-01
stops.campa: Bode writes for the proceedings of the Berlin Society of Natural Science Friends that the sun is not burning at all. It is a dark planetary body under a luminous atmosphere, with land and water, mountains and valleys, arranged like the earth. William Herschel will hold the same view, and it is the ordinary opinion of serious astronomers for another sixty years. It is wrong in every particular. The man who will refuse to name a planet after a living king believes there are valleys on the sun.
stops.quote: The sun is neither burning nor glowing, but in its essence a dark planetary body, composed like our earth of land and water, varied by mountains and valleys, and enveloped in a vaporous atmosphere.
stops.quote_source: Johann Elert Bode, in Beschaeftigungen der Berlinischen Gesellschaft Naturforschender Freunde, Bd. ii, p. 233 (1776), quoted in translation in Agnes M. Clerke, A Popular History of Astronomy During the Nineteenth Century, 4th ed. (1902), ch. II, footnote 146
suggested_refs: Beschaeftigungen der Berlinischen Gesellschaft Naturforschender Freunde, Bd. ii (1776)
sources: Agnes M. Clerke, A Popular History of Astronomy During the Nineteenth Century, 4th ed. (1902), full text verified at Project Gutenberg ebook 28247

stops.name: Berlin, the comet of January
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day
stops.campa: On the sixth of January he finds a comet, catalogued afterwards as C/1779 A1 and carrying his name alone. He is thirty-two, five years into the yearbook, seven years into Berlin, and still an assistant computer at an observatory he does not yet direct. The discovery goes into the Jahrbuch, which is by now the place where German astronomy tells itself what has happened, so that Bode is at once the man who found the comet and the man who prints the notice of it.
suggested_refs: Comet C/1779 A1 (Bode)

segments.name: The New Planet and the Naming

stops.name: Berlin, the object beyond Saturn
stops.date_confidence: Herschel's discovery is attested to 13 March 1781; the month Bode took the object up is not recorded and April is an editorial default
stops.campa: William Herschel, an organist at Bath with a homemade reflector, reports a comet in March. Bode reads the positions in Berlin, computes, and says it is not a comet: it is a planet moving in a nearly circular orbit beyond Saturn, the first planet added to the sky since antiquity. He then goes back into the old catalogues hunting the same body under other descriptions, as Edmond Halley had done with his comet, and finds it in John Flamsteed's book of 1690, entered as the star 34 Tauri. With that the orbit can be fixed.
stops.quote: A moving star that can be deemed a hitherto unknown planet-like object circulating beyond the orbit of Saturn.
stops.quote_source: as rendered in the Wikipedia article 'Uranus', citing Johann Elert Bode, Berliner Astronomisches Jahrbuch (1781), p. 210, via Ellis D. Miner, Uranus: The Planet, Rings and Satellites, p. 11. The wording could not be confirmed in Miner or in Bode's Jahrbuch; HathiTrust returned HTTP 403 and the Google Books API HTTP 429
suggested_refs: Flamsteed's 1690 entry for the star 34 Tauri, recovered by Bode as an unrecognised sighting of Uranus

stops.name: Berlin, thirty-four copper plates
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1782; no month recorded, defaulted to 01-01
stops.campa: Bode publishes Vorstellung der Gestirne auf XXXIV Kupfertafeln, thirty-four copper plates of the constellations, at thirty-five, ten years into Berlin and four years short of the directorship. It is the trial run for the atlas he will publish nineteen years later. On a plate of this kind every star has to go where the numbers put it, and the figures laid over them, the bears and the serpents and the ships, have to be drawn so that they never lie about where the stars actually are.
suggested_refs: Vorstellung der Gestirne auf XXXIV Kupfertafeln, Berlin 1782

stops.name: Berlin, the treatise of the twelfth of March
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day by Bode's own later account; note that the chronology sources misdate this proposal to 1781
stops.campa: Bode reads a paper to the Gesellschaft Naturforschender Freunde in Berlin proposing a name for Herschel's planet. Herschel has called it Georgium Sidus, after George the Third. Bode argues that the series of planet names is mythological and must stay mythological, and that Uranus, father of Saturn as Saturn is father of Jupiter, is the only name that fits the order already standing. He is arguing about a living king in a room full of Prussians, and everyone present knows it.
stops.quote: In my view, it is necessary to follow the mythology in this choice, from which the ancient names of the other planets were borrowed; for among those already known, a name taken from some remarkable person or event of modern times would stand out very strangely.
stops.quote_source: Johann Elert Bode, Von dem neu entdeckten Planeten (Berlin, 1784), p. 88, restating the argument of the March 1782 paper; German text read directly from the Bayerische Staatsbibliothek scan at archive.org/details/bub_gb_ZqA5AAAAcAAJ, translation ours
suggested_refs: The Gesellschaft Naturforschender Freunde zu Berlin, before whom the naming paper was read on 12 March 1782
sources: Bode, Von dem neu entdeckten Planeten (1784), p. 88, primary scan

stops.name: Berlin, the death of Johanna Christina
stops.date_confidence: the year 1782 is attested; no month or day is recorded and the date defaults to 1 January, so the placement of this stop after the March treatise is narrative order, not chronological order
stops.campa: Johanna Christina Lange dies. The German biography gives the year and nothing else: not the month, not the cause, not the burial. She had been married to him eight years and had borne four children, the last of them in the same year she died. Bode is thirty-five, with four small children, an observatory that expects a yearbook and a naming controversy running the length of Europe. The Jahrbuch for the following year appears on schedule, and so does every one after it.
suggested_refs: The undated 1782 death of Bode's first wife, recorded only by year

stops.name: Berlin, Von dem neu entdeckten Planeten
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1784; no month recorded, defaulted to 01-01
stops.campa: The treatise on the new planet is printed at Berlin, and in it Bode lays the whole naming argument out in order. He reaches for Diodorus Siculus and the Atlantes: Uranus their first king, founder of their settled life, inventor of many useful arts, and described besides as a diligent and skilful investigator of the heavens. Then the genealogy, which is the argument that actually works. After this book the name stops being a proposal and starts being a fact that other astronomers use.
stops.quote: Uranus was their first king, founder of their civilized life and inventor of many useful arts... Uranus was the father of Saturn and of Atlas, just as Saturn was the father of Jupiter.
stops.quote_source: Johann Elert Bode, Von dem neu entdeckten Planeten (Berlin, 1784), pp. 88 and 90, read directly from the Bayerische Staatsbibliothek scan at archive.org/details/bub_gb_ZqA5AAAAcAAJ, translation ours. The ellipsis spans two printed pages and omits Bode's remark that Uranus was also described as a diligent astronomer of antiquity
suggested_refs: Bode, Von dem neu entdeckten Planeten (Berlin, 1784), Bayerische Staatsbibliothek copy
sources: Bode, Von dem neu entdeckten Planeten (1784), primary scan at archive.org/details/bub_gb_ZqA5AAAAcAAJ

stops.name: Berlin, second marriage and a fifth child
stops.date_confidence: the son's birth year 1784 is attested; the date of the marriage to Sophie Dorothea Lange is not recorded anywhere reachable and is placed before the birth by inference only
stops.campa: Bode marries Sophie Dorothea Lange. Their son Karl Ferdinand Elert Bode is born in 1784 and lives until 1857, outliving his father by thirty-one years and every one of his half-siblings by more than forty. The marriage lasts six years. Sophie dies in 1790, and Bode, twice widowed before he is forty-four, does not marry a third time. Nothing in the reachable record says where either wife is buried, or where he lived in Berlin apart from the tower.
suggested_refs: Karl Ferdinand Elert Bode, 1784-1857, the only child to outlive his father

stops.name: St Petersburg, elected in absentia
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1785; no month recorded, defaulted to 01-01. The pin is inherited from leonard_euler.journey.json and marks Euler's last address, not any building Bode entered
stops.campa: The Imperial Academy of Sciences at Saint Petersburg elects Bode a corresponding member, and in 1794 makes him an honorary one. He never goes to Russia. Two years before the first election, Leonhard Euler had spent the last afternoon of his life in this city discussing with Anders Johan Lexell the orbit of the new planet, the one Bode had insisted was a planet and had named. The two men never meet, and never correspond in any surviving letter. The planet is in both rooms.
suggested_refs: The Imperial Academy of Sciences, St Petersburg, election records for 1785 and 1794

stops.name: Berlin, director of the observatory
stops.date_confidence: the year is attested; no month recorded, defaulted to 01-01
stops.campa: Fourteen years after arriving as Lambert's computer, Bode is made director of the Berlin Observatory and elected a full member of the Prussian Academy of Sciences. He holds the directorship thirty-nine years. He also runs the calculating institute descended from Kirch's foundation of 1700, the body later called the Astronomisches Rechen-Institut, which will move to Heidelberg after the Second World War. Tower, yearbook and institute are in practice one man with one working eye.
suggested_refs: The Astronomisches Rechen-Institut, Berlin, directed by Bode c. 1787-1825

stops.name: Berlin, Klaproth names the metal
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1789; no month recorded, defaulted to 01-01
stops.campa: Martin Heinrich Klaproth, working in Berlin, isolates a new element out of pitchblende and calls it uranium, after the planet Bode named seven years earlier. Bode had taken the word from Diodorus Siculus and pressed it on a reluctant Europe; it now sits on a chemist's shelf, in a city where the man who supplied it directs the observatory. It is still attached to the metal in 1938, and in 1945, by which time the name has stopped pointing at the sky altogether.
suggested_refs: Klaproth's 1789 isolation of uranium from pitchblende, named for the planet

stops.name: London, elected to the Royal Society
stops.date_confidence: attested to April 1789; the day is not recorded, defaulted to the first
stops.campa: The Royal Society of London elects Bode a Fellow in April. He never crosses the Channel, never sees England, and the honour reaches him by post at a tower in Dorotheenstadt. The Society had had Isaac Newton for its president; the astronomy it now rewards in Berlin is Newton's mechanics ground down into columns of predicted positions, printed annually and used by every observatory in Europe. That is what the Jahrbuch is, and it is why the elections keep arriving.
suggested_refs: Royal Society election records, April 1789

stops.name: Berlin, the second widowing
stops.date_confidence: the year is attested; no month or day recorded, defaulted to 01-01
stops.campa: Sophie Dorothea Lange dies. Bode is forty-three, twice a widower, with five children of whom four will die before him. The German biography gives the year and stops there: no month, no cause, no grave, no second sentence. What continues without a break through 1790 and every year after it is the Astronomisches Jahrbuch, computed, edited and printed on time, which is the only document of his that runs the full length of his adult life and the only one in which the household never appears at all.
suggested_refs: The undated 1790 death of Bode's second wife, recorded only by year

stops.name: Gotha, the first congress of astronomers
stops.date_confidence: attested to August 1798; no exact day recorded, defaulted to the first. Coordinates are the Seeberg observatory site as given by de.wikipedia; the atlas holds no prior Gotha pin to inherit
stops.campa: On the Seeberg hill above Gotha, in the observatory Franz Xaver von Zach built with Duke Ernst the Second's money, the astronomers of Europe meet for the first time as a body. Bode travels there and meets Jerome Lalande. It is the only journey outside the Hamburg and Berlin axis that the sources record for him, which is not the same as saying it is the only one he made. Out of Seeberg and the gatherings that follow it comes the search party for the missing planet at 28.
suggested_refs: Seeberg Observatory near Gotha, host of the first European astronomers' congress in 1798

stops.name: Berlin, the Uranographia
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1801; no month recorded, defaulted to 01-01
stops.campa: Bode publishes Uranographia sive Astrorum Descriptio, twenty large copper plates, with the companion catalogue Allgemeine Beschreibung und Nachweisung der Gestirne listing more than seventeen thousand stars. It is the last great star atlas to draw the constellation figures over accurate positions; after it the discipline gives the pictures up. Nineteen years of engraving stand behind it, back through the thirty-four plates of 1782, and behind those a boy copying charts out of a borrowed library in Hamburg.
suggested_refs: Uranographia sive Astrorum Descriptio, Berlin 1801, twenty engraved plates

stops.name: Palermo, Ceres in the gap
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1 January 1801. Coordinates are the Palermo Astronomical Observatory on the Palazzo dei Normanni, about 700 metres southwest of the city-centre point given in the research pool
stops.campa: On the first night of the new century Giuseppe Piazzi, working at the observatory on the roof of the Palazzo dei Normanni, records a moving object between Mars and Jupiter, very near where Bode's series had left its hole at 28. Piazzi loses it behind the sun after forty-one days. The law has produced, on the face of it, a prediction and a confirmation, and now the whole apparatus of European astronomy depends on somebody being able to find the thing a second time.
suggested_refs: Piazzi's observing log at the Palermo Observatory, 1 January 1801

stops.name: Brunswick, Gauss recovers the lost planet
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day
stops.campa: In Brunswick, Carl Friedrich Gauss takes Piazzi's three positions and computes an orbit from them by a method nobody else has, and von Zach finds Ceres again on the last night of the year. Gauss had worked out the same planetary spacing rule for himself as a schoolboy at the Collegium Carolinum and never printed it. The rule Bode spent thirty years promoting is rescued by a man of twenty-four who had thought of it privately at fifteen and judged it not worth publishing.
suggested_refs: Zach, Monatliche Correspondenz (1801-1802), which printed the prediction and the recovery

stops.name: Bremen, Olbers and the celestial police
stops.date_confidence: Pallas is attested to March 1802; this stop defaults to the year. Bode's role in the search group is reconstruction, not attestation: the atlas files do not state it and the credit is given variously to von Zach, to Olbers and to Bode
stops.campa: Wilhelm Olbers, a physician in Bremen who observes at night from the top of his own house, finds a second small body, Pallas, where Ceres had been. The search group that hunted the gap, later called the celestial police, is credited variously to von Zach, to Olbers and to Bode, and Bode's part in organising it is carried here as reconstruction. The single missing planet the law had demanded turns out to be rubble, which no version of the law had predicted.
suggested_refs: The Lilienthal 'celestial police' circle and the search for the planet at 28

stops.name: Berlin, the burial of the children
stops.date_confidence: the death years 1804, 1806 and 1814 are attested; no months or days are recorded and the stop defaults to the first of these years
stops.campa: Theodor Heinrich August dies in 1804, at twenty-five. Johann Christian August Wilhelm dies in 1806, at twenty-nine. Anna Ernestine Christine dies in 1814, at thirty-nine. Of the four children of the first marriage none reaches forty and none outlives the father. The Jahrbuch volumes for 1804, 1806 and 1814 were computed, edited and sent to the press in those same years, and no line in any of the three records what was happening in the house while they were being made.
suggested_refs: The Bode children's death dates as preserved only in the German biography

stops.name: Berlin, the structure of the world
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1808; no month recorded, defaulted to 01-01
stops.campa: Bode publishes Allgemeine Betrachtungen uber das Weltgebaude, a survey of the structure of the universe for general readers. He is sixty-one, and the shape of his working life has not changed since Hamburg: observe, compute, engrave, then explain it to people who will never own a telescope. Immanuel Kant at Konigsberg had published a theory of how the system formed back in 1755. Whether Bode read him is stated nowhere, and the kinship of the two projects is inference, not record.
suggested_refs: Allgemeine Betrachtungen uber das Weltgebaude, Berlin 1808

stops.name: Berlin, retirement and Encke
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1825; no month recorded, defaulted to 01-01
stops.campa: At seventy-eight Bode gives up the directorship of the observatory and of the calculating institute. Johann Franz Encke succeeds him. Encke will take the observatory out of the Dorotheenstadt tower entirely, into a new building by Karl Friedrich Schinkel near the Hallesches Tor, and in 1927 the streets around that building will be named Enckeplatz and Enckestrasse. No comparable street in Berlin carries Bode's name, though he held the post for thirty-nine years and Encke for thirty-eight.
suggested_refs: Enckeplatz and Enckestrasse, Berlin, named 1927 for Bode's successor

stops.name: Berlin, the twenty-third of November
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day. The burial place is unknown and the coordinates default to the observatory, the only Berlin point firmly anchored to him
stops.campa: Bode dies in Berlin at seventy-nine, fifty-four years after Lambert sent for him. Where he is buried is not known. The English and German biographies pass over it, the Allgemeine Deutsche Biographie gives the death date and states no burial place, the Commons category holds nothing, the Findagrave memorial returned an access error and could not be read, and the Sophienfriedhof list of notable graves of his era does not include him. The man who fixed seventeen thousand positions has no fixed position of his own.
suggested_refs: The unlocated grave of Johann Elert Bode, Berlin, 1826
sources: Allgemeine Deutsche Biographie, 'Bode, Johann Elert', via de.wikisource

stops.name: Berlin, Encke's memorial address
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1827; no month recorded, defaulted to 01-01
stops.campa: Encke delivers a Gedachtnisrede for his predecessor. The following year Alexander von Humboldt, newly returned to Berlin, talks Carl Friedrich Gauss into coming up from Gottingen for the Naturforscherversammlung, and the two of them lodge on this pin, a few streets from the tower Bode had climbed for fifty-three years. Bode has been dead one year, and Gauss, who recovered Ceres in the gap Bode's series predicted, never met him. The Jahrbuch continues under Encke's name.
suggested_refs: Encke's Gedachtnisrede on Bode, Berlin 1827

stops.name: Hamburg, a traveller passes the birthplace
stops.date_confidence: Andersen leaves Copenhagen on 16 May 1831 and is in Hamburg three days later; the day is derived from that, not stated directly
stops.campa: Hans Christian Andersen, on his first journey out of Denmark, reaches Hamburg three days after leaving Copenhagen, five years after Bode's death in Berlin. Bode had left the city in 1772 and, so far as any record shows, did not come back. The house he was born in is not identified, the school where Busch lent him a telescope is not located to a building, and the Berlin grave is not found. What is fixed is the sky he drew: seventeen thousand positions, and a word for the seventh planet.
suggested_refs: Hamburg in 1831, five years after Bode's death

stops.name: Berlin, the observatory moves to Kreuzberg
stops.date_confidence: the Schinkel building was constructed 1832-1835; the year of completion is attested, no month recorded
stops.campa: Encke's new observatory, designed by Karl Friedrich Schinkel, opens near the Hallesches Tor in Kreuzberg. The instruments move, the yearbook moves, the directorship moves, and the institution acquires an address about a kilometre and a half south of the tower where Bode worked for fifty-three years. The research pool placed this building in Mitte at 52.51 and 13.39; the German source puts it here, in Kreuzberg, and the correction is carried into the pin.
suggested_refs: Schinkel's Berlin Observatory near the Hallesches Tor, completed 1835

stops.name: Berlin, Neptune outside the series
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day
stops.campa: Johann Gottfried Galle and Heinrich d'Arrest, working from Le Verrier's prediction at the Kreuzberg observatory, find Neptune on the twenty-third of September. It sits nowhere near the distance Bode's series requires for a planet of that rank. The law that Uranus had appeared to fit and Ceres had appeared to confirm is broken by the next planet found, in the same city, by the direct successors of the man who promoted it, twenty years after his death.
suggested_refs: Galle and d'Arrest's discovery of Neptune, Berlin, 23 September 1846

stops.name: Greenwich, the almanac surrenders Georgium Sidus
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1850; no month recorded, defaulted to 01-01
stops.campa: His Majesty's Nautical Almanac Office, the last holdout in Europe, stops printing Georgium Sidus and prints Uranus. Sixty-eight years have passed since Bode read his paper to the Society of Natural Science Friends, and twenty-four since he died. It is a word he took from a Greek sky god by way of Diodorus Siculus and pressed on a continent that did not want it, and it is now on every chart in every language, including the charts of the country whose king it displaced.
suggested_refs: HM Nautical Almanac Office, which used Georgium Sidus until 1850

stops.name: Cambridge, Massachusetts, the law as a cautionary tale
stops.date_confidence: the 1898 lectures are attested to the year; the specific venue is not established and the pin marks Cambridge, Massachusetts, where Peirce's 1898 lecture series was delivered
stops.campa: Charles Sanders Peirce, lecturing in 1898, uses Bode's law as his standard example of reasoning that looks like inference and is not: a formula fitted to the numbers already in hand and then read as a law of nature. By the twentieth century the journal Icarus will stop accepting papers that propose refinements to it. A hundred and twenty-six years after the footnote, the series is taught as an example of how not to reason, and it is still called Bode's law, after a man who did not discover it.
suggested_refs: Peirce's 1898 lectures, which cite Bode's law as fallacious reasoning

stops.name: Berlin, the tower comes down
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day. Coordinates follow en.wikipedia's Berlin Observatory article and differ by about a hundred metres from the figure used for the same tower at the 1772 stop
stops.campa: On the third of July the Dorotheenstadt tower, twenty-seven metres of it, standing since 1711, is demolished. In 1914 the Prussian State Library takes the ground. Bode had worked in it from 1772 to 1825, found M81 and M82 from its roof, engraved the Uranographia inside it and computed some fifty yearbooks under it. Nothing of it stands. The two coordinate figures the sources give for the site differ by about a hundred metres and the footprint is not settled.
suggested_refs: The demolition of the Dorotheenstadt tower observatory, 3 July 1903

stops.name: Heidelberg, a body in the outer belt
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day
stops.campa: Karl Reinmuth, observing at Heidelberg, finds a dark body about thirty-one kilometres across in the outer asteroid belt. On the proposal of the Swedish astronomer Bror Asplind it is numbered 998 and named Bodea. It moves in the region Bode's series said should hold one planet and that holds instead several hundred thousand rocks. In 1935 the International Astronomical Union puts his name on a bright bowl-shaped crater on the near side of the moon, with the rilles called Rimae Bode lying west of it.
suggested_refs: Asteroid 998 Bodea, discovered at Heidelberg on 6 August 1923; the lunar crater Bode, named 1935

stops.name: Canberra, the series tested on other suns
stops.date_confidence: the study is attested to 2013; no month recorded, defaulted to 01-01. The pin marks the Australian National University, the authors' institution, which the cited source does not state explicitly
stops.campa: Timothy Bovaird and Charles Lineweaver test a generalised Titius-Bode relation against the spacing of planets in a sample of systems around other stars and report that it fits in ninety-six per cent of them. Nothing is settled by that. Whether planets pack themselves according to a rule or only look as though they do is the question Bode's footnote raised in 1772, put now to systems he had no way of knowing existed, by people using his name for a formula he did not invent.
suggested_refs: Bovaird and Lineweaver (2013) on generalised Titius-Bode relations in exoplanet systems
